title: Shloka 78
subtitle: The wish-yielding creeper, the loosened tether, and the rule of good conduct

namas.translation: For those who hold to her she is the slender celestial creeper that yields whatever is asked of it.

compound.gloss: the wish-yielding creeper of those who have devotion

namas.translation: The soul is tethered like a beast; she is the one who unties the rope.

compound.gloss: she who releases the fetter of the bound creature

children.gloss: the tether of the bound creature
a tethered animal, and so the bound soul
she who unbinds or sets free

namas.translation: Every false teaching is gathered up and put away by her, with nothing left over.

compound.gloss: by whom all heretics have been swept away

children.gloss: a heretic, a professor of false doctrine

namas.translation: She starts good behaviour moving in the world and keeps it going once it has begun.

compound.gloss: she who sets right conduct in motion

commentary.meaning: Four names, each filling exactly one quarter of the verse, and together they trace a movement outward from the single devotee to the ordering of religion at large. The first is pure gift: to those who have devotion she is the wish-yielding creeper of the gods, and the gift is unconditional except for the one condition folded into the compound, that there be devotion. The second says what the gift actually consists of, and says it in the technical vocabulary of Śaiva theology — the soul is a beast on a tether, and she is the one who unties the rope. The third and fourth leave the individual altogether and speak about the world: she has gathered up every false teaching without remainder, and she is what sets right conduct moving among people. The verse begins in grace and ends in law. A reader who takes the four in order will also notice that the hymn has quietly stopped describing her body and her ornaments and begun describing her government.
commentary.history:
Kalpalatikā is built on a stock image of Sanskrit poetry that has hardened into a single word. The root is √kḷp, to be in order, to be fit, whose causative kalpayati means to arrange or produce; a kalpa-vṛkṣa is therefore a tree that produces to order, and the celestial garden of Indra is furnished with such trees, along with the cow that gives whatever is milked from her and the jewel that grants whatever is asked of it. The purāṇas generally place these among the treasures that came up when the gods and the antigods churned the ocean, though the lists differ from one purāṇa to the next and the number of items in them is not stable. What the hymn does with the image is small and deliberate. It does not call her a tree. Latā is a creeper, latikā its diminutive: a slender climbing thing, which by its nature cannot stand up on its own and must have something to grow along. And the creeper is not simply the world's; it is bhaktimatām, of those possessed of devotion. The gift is not being restricted out of stinginess. It is being located: the creeper grows where there is something for it to climb.

The second name moves into a vocabulary that Śaiva theology had made precise centuries before this hymn was composed. Paśu is an ordinary word for a domestic animal, and behind it stands the sacrificial victim of the Vedic rite, tied by a rope to the stake. Pāśa is that rope. From at least the Pāśupata movement onward, the two words are taken as a diagram of the human condition: the soul is the tethered animal, its bondage is the tether, and the lord — pati, the third term — is the one who owns the animal and can loose it. Śaiva Siddhānta systematised the fetters as three: āṇava, the impurity that shrinks an infinite awareness to the size of a person; karma, the accumulated momentum of action; and māyā, the material stuff that gives that momentum something to work in. The name assigns to her the office that the systems assign to Śiva. She is the one who unties.

There is a second and more domestic sense of paśu that a tantric reader will hear at the same time. Tantric texts classify practitioners by temperament into paśu, vīra and divya — the herd-natured, the heroic, and the divine — and the paśu is the practitioner who is not yet fit for the transgressive rites and must be held to conventional observance. Both senses are live in this verse, and the fourth name will pick up the second one.

Pāṣaṇḍa, in the third name, is the hardest word in the verse, and its history is worth knowing before anyone decides how harsh it is. In the Prakrit of Aśoka's inscriptions the word appears as pāsaṃḍa and means simply a religious community or sect, with no pejorative charge at all; the emperor's edicts use it while enjoining that the various pāsaṃḍas be honoured and not disparaged. By the classical period the word has slid downhill and means a heretic — someone outside the Vedic fold, or a fraudulent ascetic wearing the marks of a piety he does not have. Commentators on this name generally soften it in one of two ways: by reading pāṣaṇḍa as the false doctrine rather than the person who holds it, or by pressing on saṃhṛta. That participle is from sam-√hṛ, to draw together, the same verb that gives saṃhāra, the drawing-in of the cosmos at the end of an age. Withdrawal in that sense is not extermination; it is reabsorption of something into the source it came from. Traditions differ on how much weight the milder reading can carry, and it is honest to say so.

Sadācāra, finally, is a technical term of dharmaśāstra and not a vague commendation of being good. The lawbooks list the sources from which dharma may be known, and after the Veda and the remembered texts they place ācāra, the settled practice of people who are themselves good — precedent, in effect, where scripture is silent. Pravartikā is from pra-√vṛt in the causative: she who sets rolling. The pairing matters for a tantric hymn, because Śrīvidyā has an internal argument between the samaya lineages, which keep the rite interior and the conduct orthodox, and the kaula lineages, which do not. The sahasranāma itself carries names from both vocabularies and does not resolve the quarrel; Lakṣmīdhara's well-known commentary on the Saundaryalaharī takes the samaya side vigorously and reads the poem against kaula practice throughout. Whatever a given lineage decides, the name insists that liberation from the tether is not the end of the matter, and that the goddess who unties the rope is also the one who keeps ordinary decency in motion.
commentary.practice:
Metrically this is the easiest verse in a long stretch of the hymn, and it is worth noticing why. Each of the four names is exactly eight syllables, so each fills one quarter of the anuṣṭubh exactly. Nothing spans the caesura, nothing has to be split across a breath. The units of sense and the units of metre coincide four times over, which means the verse can be chanted at speed without any of the place-losing that afflicts the mahā- runs earlier in the stotra.

The real work here is sibilants. Sanskrit has three — dental s, palatal ś, and retroflex ṣ — and saṃhṛtāśeṣapāṣaṇḍā contains all three in a single word, in the order s, ś, ṣ, ṣ. Say it slowly: saṃ with the tongue nowhere near the roof of the mouth and the sibilant at the teeth; śe with the blade of the tongue at the hard palate, close to the English sh but further forward; ṣa with the tongue tip curled back. English collapses the last two into one sound and will do so here unless you deliberately keep them apart. Paśupāśavimocinī gives you the palatal twice with nothing else to confuse it, so it makes a useful warm-up: run paśu-pāśa a few times to fix ś, then take up the longer name.

Two further points of articulation. The hṛ of saṃhṛta carries the vocalic ṛ, which is a vowel in its own right with the tongue in retroflex position — not the ri of English "rip", and not a schwa with an r after it. And ṇḍā at the end of the same word is a retroflex nasal followed by a retroflex stop, both made with the tongue curled back; the whole final third of the word is produced in that one position, which is why it feels like a knot and why slowing down there is the only cure. In pravartikā the r closes and the following t is dental, so the tongue moves forward, not back.

Used as archanā, the four names take the dative: bhaktimatkalpalatikāyai namaḥ, paśupāśavimocinyai namaḥ, saṃhṛtāśeṣapāṣaṇḍāyai namaḥ, sadācārapravartikāyai namaḥ. Three of the four are ā-stems and take the familiar -āyai. The second is an ī-stem, and its dative is -yai attached directly, giving vimocinyai — the same pattern that appears throughout the hymn wherever a name ends in -inī, and a good place to hear the difference between the two declensions in immediate succession.

As for what the verse asks of the person saying it: the second name requires you to accept a description of yourself as an animal on a rope, which is not flattering and is not meant to be. The fourth then withholds the consolation that might follow. Having been untied, one might expect to be told that conduct no longer matters. Instead the verse ends by making her the source of ordinary right behaviour, which is to say that the loosened rope leads back into the world rather than out of it.

crossReferences.iast: śaraṇāgatadīnārtaparitrāṇaparāyaṇe | sarvasyārtihare devi nārāyaṇi namo'stu te ||
crossReferences.translation: You whose whole occupation is the rescue of the wretched and the suffering who have come to you for shelter, you who take away the distress of everything that exists — Nārāyaṇī, goddess, homage to you.
crossReferences.relevance: The plainest statement of the logic behind bhaktimatkalpalatikā. What qualifies a person for her help is not merit or learning but the act of coming to her; the wish-yielding creeper grows where there is something for it to climb.

crossReferences.translation: When the god is known, every fetter falls away; the afflictions wear out and birth and death are done with. From meditation upon him there comes, at the parting from the body, a third state — sovereignty over all, and, alone, the fulfilment of every desire.
crossReferences.relevance: The upaniṣadic ancestor of paśupāśavimocinī. The vocabulary of pāśa as the thing that binds a soul, and of knowledge of the deity as what makes it drop, is already fully formed here, several centuries before the Śaiva systems that will turn paśu, pāśa and pati into a formal triad.

crossReferences.deva: वेदः स्मृतिः सदाचारः स्वस्य च प्रियमात्मनः । एतच्चतुर्विधं प्राहुः साक्षाद्धर्मस्य लक्षणम् ॥
crossReferences.iast: vedaḥ smṛtiḥ sadācāraḥ svasya ca priyam ātmanaḥ | etac caturvidhaṃ prāhuḥ sākṣād dharmasya lakṣaṇam ||
crossReferences.translation: The Veda, the remembered texts, the conduct of good people, and what is agreeable to one's own self: these four, they say, are the direct marks by which dharma is known.
crossReferences.relevance: Shows that sadācāra in the fourth name is a term of art rather than a compliment. It names one of the recognised sources of law — the settled practice of the good, appealed to precisely where scripture gives no ruling — and to make her its pravartikā is to make her the origin of a source of authority, not merely a well-behaved deity.

references.title: Lalitā-Sahasranāma, with Bhāskararāya's commentary Saubhāgyabhāskara
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Adyar Library / Theosophical Publishing House)
references.note: The standard English window onto the commentarial tradition, and the first place to look when a name like saṃhṛtāśeṣapāṣaṇḍā seems harsher than the surrounding hymn. Read it knowing that Bhāskararāya argues rather than reports; his readings are one learned eighteenth-century view, not the tradition's unanimous voice.

references.title: Auspicious Wisdom: The Texts and Traditions of Śrīvidyā Śākta Tantrism in South India
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (SUNY Press, 1992)
references.note: The clearest account of the samaya and kaula division inside this tradition, which is the argument sitting underneath sadācārapravartikā. Brooks is good on why a tantric lineage would want to be conspicuously orthodox in public and what that costs it.

references.title: Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas
references.author: Romila Thapar (Oxford University Press, 3rd ed. 2012)
references.note: Includes translations of the edicts, where pāsaṃḍa still means simply a religious community and the emperor asks that all of them be treated with respect. Useful here for one reason only, but a decisive one: it shows that the word in the third name had no insult in it for several centuries before it acquired one.

references.title: Manu's Code of Law: A Critical Edition and Translation of the Mānava-Dharmaśāstra
references.author: Patrick Olivelle (Oxford University Press, 2005)
references.note: For the second chapter, where the sources of dharma are set out and sadācāra is given its place among them. Olivelle's introduction on how ācāra actually functioned — as precedent filling the gaps left by scripture — explains what pravartikā is claiming better than any devotional gloss will.

references.title: A Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899)
references.note: Worth opening at pāśa and at pāṣaṇḍa in the same sitting. The entries lay out the range from sacrificial rope to Varuṇa's noose to metaphysical bondage, and the second shows the pejorative sense arriving late and unevenly.
